summary.text: The cases $n=2,3$ are settled by finite minimality checks, while for $n=4$ the congruences of a number and its reversal modulo $81$, together with the relation between their weighted digit sums, force any smaller positive candidate to have digit sum $81$ and hence to be nine 9s.  For $n=5,6$ explicit smaller bidivisible candidates rule out equality, and for all larger $n$ a recursively repeated three-block decimal construction makes both the number and its reversal divisible by the required power of $3$ (each repetition contributes a factor $1+10^M+10^{2M}$ divisible by $3$) while remaining below the all-nines target.

full_proof.text:
Let \(R(x)\) denote the integer obtained by reversing the usual base-10 digits of \(x\). Leading zeroes created by the reversal are discarded, as usual. For a positive integer \(m\), the definition of \(a(m)\) can equivalently be written
\[
a(m)=\min\{C>0:m\mid C\text{ and }m\mid R(C)\},
\]
provided this set is nonempty; if it is empty, the value is \(0\). Indeed, the formal definition searches for the least positive multiplier \(k\) such that \(m\mid R(km)\), and then returns \(km\).

We prove that, for every \(n\geq 2\),
\[
a(3^n)=10^{3^{n-2}}-1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
n\in\{2,3,4\}.
\]

## 1. The three exceptional exponents

### The case \(n=2\)

Here \(3^n=9\). The number \(9\) is divisible by \(9\), and its reversal is again \(9\). Since it is already the first positive multiple of \(9\),
\[
a(9)=9=10^{3^0}-1.
\]

### The case \(n=3\)

Here \(3^n=27\). The multiplier \(37\) gives
\[
37\cdot 27=999,
\]
and \(R(999)=999\), so \(999\) is admissible.

It remains to show that none of the positive multipliers \(1,2,\ldots,36\) works. The following table gives \(R(27k)\pmod {27}\) for those multipliers, grouped nine at a time:
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrrr}
k&1&2&3&4&5&6&7&8&9\\ \hline
R(27k)\bmod 27&18&18&18&18&18&18&9&18&18
\end{array}
\]
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrrr}
k&10&11&12&13&14&15&16&17&18\\ \hline
R(27k)\bmod 27&18&9&18&18&9&18&18&9&9
\end{array}
\]
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrrr}
k&19&20&21&22&23&24&25&26&27\\ \hline
R(27k)\bmod 27&18&18&9&9&18&9&9&18&9
\end{array}
\]
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrrr}
k&28&29&30&31&32&33&34&35&36\\ \hline
R(27k)\bmod 27&9&9&18&9&9&9&9&9&9.
\end{array}
\]
Thus no such reversal is divisible by \(27\). For \(k=37\), the residue is \(0\), because the number is \(999\). Hence
\[
a(27)=999=10^3-1=10^{3^1}-1.
\]

### The case \(n=4\): determination of \(a(81)\)

We now prove
\[
a(81)=999999999=10^9-1.
\]
The number on the right is admissible, because
\[
999999999=81\cdot 12345679
\]
and its reversal is itself. The substantive point is that no smaller positive multiple of \(81\) can have a reversal also divisible by \(81\).

Suppose, to the contrary, that \(M\) is positive, that
\[
81\mid M,\qquad 81\mid R(M),
\]
and that \(M<999999999<10^9\). Write the decimal digits of \(M\), starting with the units digit, as
\[
L=(d_0,d_1,\ldots,d_{\ell-1}).
\]
Thus
\[
M=\sum_{i=0}^{\ell-1}d_i10^i,
\]
where \(0\leq d_i\leq9\), \(d_{\ell-1}\neq0\), and, because \(M<10^9\),
\[
1\leq \ell\leq9.
\]
Define
\[
S=\sum_{i=0}^{\ell-1}d_i,
\qquad
W=\sum_{i=0}^{\ell-1}i d_i.
\]
Since \(10=1+9\), the binomial theorem gives
\[
10^i=(1+9)^i\equiv 1+9i\pmod {81};
\]
all terms of binomial degree at least two contain a factor \(9^2=81\). Consequently
\[
M\equiv S+9W\pmod {81}. \tag{1}
\]

The least-significant-first digit list for the reversed number is the reverse of \(L\). Let
\[
W'=\sum_{i=0}^{\ell-1}i d_{\ell-1-i}

after reindexing the reversed list. The same congruence gives
\[
R(M)\equiv S+9W'\pmod {81}. \tag{2}
\]
For each original digit \(d_i\), its index in the reversed list is \(\ell-1-i\). Therefore
\[
W+W'=\sum_{i=0}^{\ell-1}\bigl(i+(\ell-1-i)\bigr)d_i
=(\ell-1)S. \tag{3}
\]

Both \(M\) and \(R(M)\) are divisible by \(81\). Adding (1) and (2), then using (3), yields
\[
0\equiv 2S+9(W+W')
=S\bigl(2+9(\ell-1)\bigr)\pmod {81}. \tag{4}
\]
For \(1\leq\ell\leq9\), the second factor in (4) is respectively
\[
2,11,20,29,38,47,56,65,74.
\]
Every one of these is congruent to \(2\pmod3\), and hence each is relatively prime to \(81=3^4\). It follows from (4) that
\[
81\mid S.
\]
On the other hand, \(M>0\), so at least one digit is nonzero and \(S>0\), while
\[
S\leq9\ell\leq81.
\]
Thus \(S=81\). Equality throughout forces \(\ell=9\), and nine decimal digits, each at most \(9\), can have sum \(81\) only if every digit is \(9\). Hence
\[
M=999999999,
\]
contrary to the assumed strict inequality.

Thus \(999999999\) is the least admissible multiple of \(81\), and
\[
a(81)=999999999=10^9-1=10^{3^2}-1.
\]
This completes the proof of the equality for \(n=2,3,4\).

## 2. Explicit failures for \(n=5\) and \(n=6\)

For \(n=5\), so that \(3^n=243\), take
\[
C_5=4899999987.
\]
Direct division and reversal give
\[
C_5=243\cdot20164609,
\]
\[
R(C_5)=7899999984=243\cdot32510288.
\]
Thus \(C_5\) is an admissible multiple of \(243\). Moreover
\[
C_5<10^{27}-1.
\]
Therefore the least admissible multiple satisfies
\[
a(243)\leq C_5<10^{27}-1,
\]
so
\[
a(3^5)\neq10^{3^3}-1.
\]

For \(n=6\), take
\[
C_6=19899999972.
\]
Here
\[
C_6=729\cdot27297668,
\]
and
\[
R(C_6)=27999999891=729\cdot38408779.
\]
Thus this is admissible for \(729=3^6\), and plainly
\[
C_6<10^{81}-1.
\]
It follows that
\[
a(3^6)\neq10^{3^4}-1.
\]

We next construct admissible numbers uniformly for every exponent at least \(7\).

## 3. A repeated-block reversal identity

We first record a decimal fact. Let \(M>0\), let \(N\) be a positive integer, and suppose \(M<10^N\). Then
\[
R\!\left(M(1+10^N+10^{2N})\right)
=R(M)(1+10^N+10^{2N}). \tag{5}
\]

To see this carefully, let the least-significant-first digit list of \(M\) be \(A\), of length \(\ell\leq N\), and put \(k=N-\ell\). Since the three shifted copies occupy disjoint blocks of \(N\) decimal positions, the least-significant-first digit list of
\[
M+M10^N+M10^{2N}

after padding the first two blocks to length \(N\), is
\[
A,\underbrace{0,\ldots,0}_{k},
A,\underbrace{0,\ldots,0}_{k},A.
\]
Reversing this list gives
\[
A^{\mathrm{rev}},\underbrace{0,\ldots,0}_{k},
A^{\mathrm{rev}},\underbrace{0,\ldots,0}_{k},A^{\mathrm{rev}}.
\]
The numerical value of \(A^{\mathrm{rev}}\) is \(R(M)\), and the padding makes the offsets between the three copies exactly \(N\). The value of the reversed list is therefore
\[
R(M)+R(M)10^N+R(M)10^{2N},
\]
which proves (5). This argument also handles zeroes at either end of the original decimal representation, because the inserted padding records the full block width.

We will also use the elementary identity
\[
(10^N-1)(1+10^N+10^{2N})=10^{3N}-1. \tag{6}
\]
Finally,
\[
3\mid 1+10^N+10^{2N} \tag{7}
\]
for every \(N\), since \(10\equiv1\pmod3\), making the right-hand side congruent to \(1+1+1=0\pmod3\).

## 4. The uniform family of smaller admissible numbers

Define a sequence \(W_d\) for \(d\geq0\) by
\[
W_0=4899999987
\]
and
\[
W_{d+1}=W_d\left(1+10^{10\cdot3^d}+10^{20\cdot3^d}\right). \tag{8}
\]
Thus each step repeats the preceding decimal block three times, with block width \(10\cdot3^d\).

We prove simultaneously the three properties needed later:
\[
0<W_d<10^{10\cdot3^d}, \tag{9}
\]
\[
3^{d+5}\mid W_d, \tag{10}
\]
and
\[
3^{d+5}\mid R(W_d). \tag{11}
\]

Positivity is immediate from (8), since the initial value and every factor are positive.

For the upper bound (9), the base case is the direct inequality
\[
4899999987<10^{10}.
\]
Suppose it holds for \(d\), and put
\[
N=10\cdot3^d.
\]
Because \(W_d\) is an integer and \(W_d<10^N\), we have \(W_d\leq10^N-1\). Hence, using (6),
\[
\begin{aligned}
W_{d+1}
&=W_d(1+10^N+10^{2N})\\
&\leq(10^N-1)(1+10^N+10^{2N})\\
&=10^{3N}-1<10^{3N}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since
\[
3N=3(10\cdot3^d)=10\cdot3^{d+1},
\]
this is exactly (9) for \(d+1\).

For (10), the base calculation already made above is
\[
W_0=4899999987=3^5\cdot20164609.
\]
If \(3^{d+5}\mid W_d\), then by (7), with \(N=10\cdot3^d\), the additional factor in (8) is divisible by \(3\). Therefore
\[
3^{d+6}\mid W_{d+1},
\]
which proves (10) by induction.

For the reversals, first note that
\[
R(W_0)=7899999984=3^5\cdot32510288.
\]
By (9), \(W_d<10^N\) for \(N=10\cdot3^d\), so the repeated-block identity (5) applies to (8) and gives
\[
R(W_{d+1})
=R(W_d)(1+10^N+10^{2N}). \tag{12}
\]
Starting from the displayed divisibility of \(R(W_0)\), equation (7) and induction in (12) show that each step supplies one further factor of \(3\). Thus
\[
3^{d+5}\mid R(W_d),
\]
proving (11).

## 5. Failure for every exponent at least \(7\)

Let \(e\geq7\). Write
\[
e=r+7
\]
with \(r\geq0\), and set
\[
d=r+2=e-5.
\]
Then (10) and (11) say
\[
3^e=3^{d+5}\mid W_d,
\qquad
3^e\mid R(W_d).
\]
Thus \(W_d\) is an admissible positive number in the definition of \(a(3^e)\).

It is also strictly smaller than the proposed all-nines number. Indeed, by (9),
\[
W_d<10^{10\cdot3^d}.
\]
The exponent in the conjectured value is
\[
3^{e-2}=3^{d+3}=27\cdot3^d.
\]
Since \(10<27\) and \(3^d>0\),
\[
10\cdot3^d<27\cdot3^d=3^{e-2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
10^{10\cdot3^d}<10^{3^{e-2}}.
\]
Both sides are integers, so
\[
10^{10\cdot3^d}\leq10^{3^{e-2}}-1.
\]
Combining this with the strict bound on \(W_d\), we obtain
\[
W_d<10^{3^{e-2}}-1.
\]
Since \(a(3^e)\) is the least admissible positive multiple and \(W_d\) is admissible,
\[
a(3^e)\leq W_d<10^{3^{e-2}}-1.
\]
Consequently the proposed equality fails for every \(e\geq7\).

## 6. Conclusion

For \(n=2,3,4\), the exact calculations above give respectively
\[
a(3^2)=9=10^{3^0}-1,
\]
\[
a(3^3)=999=10^{3^1}-1,
\]
and
\[
a(3^4)=999999999=10^{3^2}-1.
\]
For \(n=5\) and \(n=6\), the explicit admissible numbers \(C_5\) and \(C_6\) are strictly below the proposed targets. For every \(n\geq7\), the corresponding number \(W_{n-5}\) is an admissible number strictly below the proposed target. Hence, for all integers \(n\geq2\),
\[
a(3^n)=10^{3^{n-2}}-1
\quad\text{if and only if}\quad
n=2,\ 3,\text{ or }4.
\]
